questions.learningObjective: apply the doctrine of defences to formation to a concrete legal fact pattern
questions.stem: Consider this: A party induced by a false statement seeks to rescind the agreement. The fraud concerned a minor detail. Which statement best states the governing legal rule on these facts?

options.text: A false statement made after the contract is formed is fraud in the inducement on these facts.
A contract may be avoided for fraudulent misrepresentation when a false statement of material fact was made with intent to induce reliance and the other party justifiably relied on it on these facts.
Any inaccurate statement, however trivial, makes the contract void on these facts.
A sincere expression of opinion about value is fraudulent if the buyer later disagrees on these facts.

questions.explanation: Fraud attacks the validity of assent. The falsehood must be material and made with the intent to induce agreement, and the victim must have relied on it reasonably, so the law distinguishes it from mere puffery or later nonperformance. Here the decisive point is misrepresentation and fraud, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.
questions.hint: Ask whether the statement was false, material and actually relied on. Keep the inquiry on misrepresentation and fraud.

options.text: A hard bargain or aggressive negotiation is duress under the circumstances described.
Only a threat of bodily harm can support a duress claim under the circumstances described.

questions.learningObjective: apply the doctrine of defences to formation to a concrete legal fact pattern
questions.stem: Picture this: A minor buying a car claims fraud in the inducement. The minor had lied about their age. On these facts, which statement about the governing principle is sound?

options.text: A false statement made after the contract is formed is fraud in the inducement on these facts.
A contract may be avoided for fraudulent misrepresentation when a false statement of material fact was made with intent to induce reliance and the other party justifiably relied on it on these facts.
Any inaccurate statement, however trivial, makes the contract void on these facts.
A sincere expression of opinion about value is fraudulent if the buyer later disagrees on these facts.

questions.explanation: Fraud attacks the validity of assent. The falsehood must be material and made with the intent to induce agreement, and the victim must have relied on it reasonably, so the law distinguishes it from mere puffery or later nonperformance. Here the decisive point is misrepresentation and fraud, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.
questions.hint: Ask whether the statement was false, material and actually relied on. Keep the inquiry on misrepresentation and fraud.

options.text: A unilateral mistake always entitles the mistaken party to rescind as this record presents them.
A bad bargain is a mistake that supports rescission as this record presents them.

A mutual mistake about a basic assumption can make a contract voidable, while a unilateral mistake usually does not unless the other party knew or should have known of it as this record presents them.
A mistake about an unimportant detail always voids the agreement as this record presents them.
options.misconception: assumes any mistake cancels a contract

questions.explanation: The law distinguishes shared and one-sided errors. When both parties share a mistaken assumption about a core fact, there is no real meeting of minds, but a single party's error is normally left where it falls. Here the decisive point is mistake and its effect on assent, so the result follows from that doctrine rather than from the surface appeal of a competing statement. Each distractor rests on a different mistake about how the doctrine operates.
questions.hint: Ask whether both parties were mistaken about the same basic fact. Keep the inquiry on mistake and its effect on assent.
